interactions.title: Rai and Dimitaur in remembered stories
lines: Kenzo: Kenzo also has been, like, absolutely like playing with his [garbled], playing with, you know, the stone that he carries. And he looks at all of you and he says, “I have a question for you all. What do you know about the Great War? What do you know about the great hero, the mage Rai?”
((Looking for notes and resolving knowledge checks))

Delwath: I've heard of him. He was well known amongst the wise at the time the Great War, always traveling with the three companions. I never knew him except as rumor and and legend and tales that were told as—as he led the—some of the battles against Cha'mutte. I know he was of elven blood, although not familiar elf.
Delwath: And all of the heroes—of all of the four heroes had vanished—well, no, actually nevermind Delwath wouldn’t know that.
DM: No cuz you vanish before they did.
Delwath: What—what became of them I—I know not—the...
Delwath: The days were dark at the time, I—the battle was won, but at what cost?

Seeker: A—I recall... I have not formally studied this particular historical character, but I do recall a tale from childhood of the adventures of Rai and Dimitaur. I always—I always thought maybe that this was purely invented. I mean there, how could such an important and great historical figure, a powerful mage such as this one, have had such a sarcastic and foul-mouthed companion? But I have fond memory of the stories of Rai and...
Kenzo: What—what? Tell me more about...

Seeker: Well, if I recall correctly, the story is actually told from Dimitaur's perspective, trying to—and this is perhaps one of those jokes in the story for the adults more than for the child—of trying to make right the historical wrongdoing of Dimitaur as, in fact, the true hero of the Great War, that it was Dimitaur, in fact, who made the crucial blow on Cha'mutte. So I don't know if there's any sort of grain of historical accuracy in that story, or if it was—if it was simply a tale for children.
Kenzo: Remember what it would look like, this, this this creature?

Seeker: Oh yes. That was a wonderful part of the story is just a description. In order to describe Dimitaur’s spectacular feats of glory, it had to be emphasized that he was, you know, the size of a small bird of prey, perhaps, with leathery skin and purple scales.
Kenzo: When you say purple scales, you see Kenzo, like...
Seeker: Cleverest potty mouth lizard. Can fly very dexterously, if the stories are to be believed.
Kenzo: What do you know, Wellby?
Wellby: Nothing more than the stories everyone knows.

before: Kenzo: And then, and how far are we from the monastery now?
DM: Like five miles. You're close.

Kenzo: So then, so is—is—we're kind of sitting, sitting in the circle, and just you've noticed in general for this this past like stretch of days has been distracted, has been like kind of someplace else, just thinking about something, engrossed in something. He's spending a lot of time meditating, I just guess. You know, there's kind of time to spare, you know, Kenzo you'll find him just kind of sitting, sitting and kind of just deep meditation, sometimes enough that you can you know again like kind of feel—feel like brief, brief trembles of the earth around him. Or, as you've seen in the past, that kind of flashing eyes, just sort of you know, clearly, clearly like ruminating on something very heavily.

Kenzo: And as we all sit in a circle in the afternoon shade, Kenzo is, you know, ate—ate the lunch, again has been very grateful for the—for the food and for—I'm assuming Delwath does most, most of our cooking, yeah? And so, you know, grateful for the meal, but also like just very, very deep and kind of lost in thought.

Kenzo: And, you know, Kenzo sort of lift his head up in—for a moment, is like there is really, really there with you all—that kind of looks at all of you, just sort of waiting, just making sure that you all can like kind of see see that he has something to say. On—so it kind of gets everybody's attention, or just sort of sitting there waiting until till everybody certain that this is that he's picking up on.
after: Kenzo: So it's been troubling me for some time. As you know, I—my, my whole reason, my own motivation of coming to the Karawa... Because you all remember I've had these strange dreams ever since I can remember the places that I've never been, or—never—I can't ever remember going into these places, but I feel like I was there. Very striking images of of places that don't don't seem to make any sense to me.
Kenzo: When I came to Karawa, and that's when I first met Candrosa. We—he brought me to to to—was it the oasis that he brought me to, you...?
DM: No, the top of the mesa.

Kenzo: He brought me to the top of the mesa, and he used the staff, which, again, I said—shared, I believe it's a way to connect this material world to the dream world. And using the staff under Candrosa’s guidance, I—I believe I entered into the dream world, and when I was there I encountered a robed figure.

Kenzo: Well, first—first, I encountered—I saw jade hand reaching towards me, which, again, I feel like I've been carrying with me something, a piece that I didn't know where it came from nor what it was a part of. And when I put the piece in the hand, suddenly I was pulled into what I believe to be the dream world.

interactions.title: Kenzo recounts the dream and the jade’s possible history

And when I put the piece in the hand, suddenly I was pulled into what I believe to be the dream world.

Kenzo: When I was there, there was a robed figure who I don't remember much of our interaction other than he told me—well, he said specifically to seek the Order of the Awakened Soul, is what he told me. That information by itself wasn't meaningful to me and so very recently, when we were with Pava and—what’s the name of the other gentleman? Pava?

Kenzo: Pava and Avaras. When we were with Pava and Avaras, they, like me, also study the occult; they are part of the larger Lakan Mystai and—but again, they state their order serves Bhishma, the monastery that we're going to go investigate shortly.

Kenzo: When I spoke with them, that's when I asked them—ask them, “Have you heard of this Order of the Awakened Soul?” And they looked at me in surprise and said, “We are the Order of the Awakened Soul.” The Order of the Awakened Soul is in fact the Order of Bhishma that is connected to this monastery. And so—so the monastery is somehow critical to not only my past but also what’s unfolding.
Kenzo: And the other, I think, connection to this and why I asked about Rai: I told you that before we left Karawa—so, I was very, very—I was very keen to use that mirror. You remember?

Kenzo: So I use the mirror, and I used it with this piece to try to understand its history and where it came from. A few different pictures of the images, but perhaps the most important image: a dragon, the shadow of a dragon cast over the land, perched above on, on a mountaintop.
Kenzo: That dragon is... That shadow is only one shadow and that I think it could be. So...

Kenzo: I don't know how this has come into my possession. I don't know exactly how this connects, but I think part of what's gone wrong, part of what's happened... In my orders history, we do know a little bit about—some about Rai. One thing we knew about him—these are also rumors, legends—was that as part of his casualty of war, as part of what he sacrificed—his—all the great heroes sacrifice—the use of his power was somehow connected to his transmutation into stone, in particular into jade.

Kenzo: No one knows if that—what—how, how much that was driven to completion, if he remains someplace, if he was—if he died like the rest of the heroes. But given what's occurred, what's been unfolding, I think part of the puzzle, part of what's happening, is that somehow over the past 200 years, each of the great heroes may have been involved in some other action that we can't see, that we can't fully understand. But I think I believe Rai had—may have been a part of providing some form of protection, or holding at bay some kind of energy or some type of evil...

Kenzo: That we may not fully comprehend. And that somehow either he was broken or something has occurred to create these pieces, and I have one, and I've carried this one with me my entire life. Somehow it's brought me close—closer, I think, to whatever latent energy or consciousness that may still exist, perhaps in the dream world. I don't know.

Kenzo: But it wasn't until—until just recently that I think I understand now that, if I did interact with him in the dream world, that that was him, if I had been carrying a piece of him somehow, that this monastery and the Order of the Awakened Soul, I think, may take on a greater significance than we may have realized.

before: Seeker: Oh yes. That was a wonderful part of the story is just a description. In order to describe Dimitaur’s spectacular feats of glory, it had to be emphasized that he was, you know, the size of a small bird of prey, perhaps, with leathery skin and purple scales.
Kenzo: When you say purple scales, you see Kenzo, like...
Seeker: Cleverest potty mouth lizard. Can fly very dexterously, if the stories are to be believed.
Kenzo: What do you know, Wellby?
Wellby: Nothing more than the stories everyone knows.
after: Seeker: Transmutation into stone?
Kenzo: Into jade, [garbled].
Seeker: Tim, do I know of significance of jade as something to be transmuted into, or association with a particular type of power?
Unknown: So.

DM: Ah, jade, not specifically. Um, you do—you do know, you are aware of a sort of general class of magic's that are more rumored than the known in general, that are—that are powered by by gemstones. So the most—the most well known is chalyte, which is itself a magical gemstone—is used—back to our—that was considered a bit dicey to use because it can have negative effects on the user, but it's often used to create magic items.

interactions.title: The shard’s appearance, magic, and family provenance
lines: Seeker: So you think this piece of jade you've got, Kenzo, this is actually part of Rai’s body? Is there any clue on it as to where? Does it have any surface detail or other features? Does it look like a broken shard, or...?

DM: I mean, so the one detail is—and you examine this before, Seeker—is that there's—there is like an outer surface. It looks like there's a smooth outer surface, and then are jagged, are—so it's like it's like a almost like a try—it's like a wedge shaped like this, where there's—well, not exactly a wedge, but there's that smooth part of them, the other side's are rougher, like it was broken from something like one—one of the faces is more smooth and weathered, but it's hard to say. Like, there's no there's no like fingernail or, you know, eyelash or anything like that—that...
DM: It's not like a piece of a finger that was broken off, or anything quite so obvious.
Kenzo: Shard. You sensed it when we first met.
Delwath: Don't remember that. Tim, is there something I should be...?
Kenzo: I think you just—you just said like there was a very strong magic item.
Delwath: Oh, I remember. I remember, yes, that it reminded me of elven magic.
Delwath: Magic that the elves use to build their cities and hide themselves from the world, and otherwise make home home.
Kenzo: I believe, I have an intuition somehow, that there's more than one of these.
Seeker: I mean, if you take the case of Arcus, the guys—the Chardonian guy turned to stone that we found...
Seeker: Dropped Arcus off a cliff, shattered him in 2000 pieces, put them back together again, it's not clear to me that we would get Arcus back. But perhaps this is a different kind of story.

Kenzo: I—it's so hard for me to say, but I think now, over the past number of months, I feel more and more sure that this piece is either directly a part of him or deeply connected in some way. And somehow, wherever he is, if he's in a dream world, which I believe may be the case, somehow the game of god's, the game of demigods that's unfolding beyond our eyes, I believe he's involved. I believe he's a—he's a player somehow.
((Speculation about the heroes’ sources of power))
Seeker: And you have no idea where you got this thing from, Kenzo?
Seeker: Bestowed upon you at birth?
Seeker: Have we heard the story of your parents, Kenzo?
Kenzo: It's not much to say. They died when I was young. I grew up on the streets in Chardon. Is the only piece of value that I had my entire life.
Seeker: Would they have passed it down from their parents, or stolen it?

Kenzo: Know [garbled]. When I use the mirror, one image that I saw was a man in the desert giving them this piece. I don't know if it was barter and exchange. When we go back to Karawa, I'd like—I'd like to try to mirror with the piece. But this, this stone has much history that I think is important to what’s unfolding.

Kenzo: So the monastery that we journey to is in fact the monastery of the Order of the Awakened Soul. And if the man in my vision was in fact either a dream world version of Rai—and then I suppose it could be a trap, to—but I don't know. It's a monastery is significant.

DM: But there are rumors and stories of sort of pure forms of gemstone magic, where the crystalline structure of certain geological—certain minerals—can enhance or can resonate with certain magical energies.
after: Seeker: The Order of Bhishma shepherds the dead to a peaceful afterlife. Is that seem correct?

Kenzo: Yes, and but, but the order has changed. What, what—what's done now is a mere shadow of what once was the Order of the Awakened Soul, how—certainly what what's done is is care for the bodies, but the order in the past, I think, had much greater ambition, was involved in much, much more significant enterprises. Tim, I'm now forgetting exactly what those...
DM: So, that...
Kenzo: Would you—wait, did they tell me? They told—Pava...?

DM: Pava told you that in ancient days the order was charged with recording and sharing the stories of the people of Dunmar. Right, and then so many died at that—so many died unburied that they kind of changed their focus after the Great War.

after: Kenzo: Wellby.
Wellby: Think we should start in the Hall of Stories, in the tower, at dusk. Dusk? Well, I mean, maybe not; that may make it more difficult on the inside, but...
Delwath: Was there any signs of life?
Wellby: No, nothing in the in this complex, right?
DM: Um, nothing in this complex, although, ah, it was also the hottest part of the day, and you didn't look inside any buildings.

interactions.title: Agata and Shakun on the remembered timeline
lines: Delwath: But, like, Agata Dustmother predates 30 years.
DM: Yeah, it goes all the way back to the end of the Great War.
Seeker: And the the fall of the protection of Shakun...
DM: Six months in the last year.
DM: So if you were to just look at everything that's happened and say when did something change, it would be like nine to 12 months ago, not 30 years ago.

before: Kenzo: Nonfungible, right?
Unknown: Yeah.
Delwath: NFTs.
Delwath: Okay, but we don't know like nothing happened with the ship, to—none of that stuff was 30 years ago.

DM: As far as you know, the timeline is roughly a—Great War, a bunch of hobgoblin wars and stuff after, like the stuff in Raven’s Hold. Then kind of nothing for a while, then this thing 30 years ago, then kind of nothing for a while. And then within the last year, a lot of stuff seems to have started happening.
after: Seeker: I don't remember why that event 30 years ago, like the what the monks were trying to—put problem they're trying to solve. We don't have some emerging...?
DM: Nobody knows—the—nobody who was a master survived. Pava and Avaras were not masters at the time, and the masters had concocted some secret plan and all left.
Delwath: Do we know in what fashion everybody else who has gone to investigate this has died horribly?
Kenzo: And never come back.
DM: They never come back.

interactions.title: Bhishma, awakened souls, and the gods
lines: Seeker: Kenzo, what does it mean to awaken a soul? Hmm, that's what I was getting at with the Order of Bhishma. They—they let people go to heaven. They don't resurrect them or something, do they? That's what I associate with awakening souls.
Delwath: In ancient elven tradition, awakening souls was what the—was what the great powers did before the gods, to awaken the trees and the animals and the giant eagles.
Seeker: Are you suggesting, though, is that the awakening of souls is not the awakening of souls of people, but of other things?
Seeker: And surely this would be reflected in the story of Bhishma.
Delwath: I don't think it's what these people were doing, at least not what they would have... Does not feel like a human thing.
Seeker: Did Bhishma resurrect or otherwise awaken anyone in the story of...?
Delwath: He brought the god who died to save the Dunmari back to life.
Seeker: He brought Jeevali back. Well, there's your answer, I suppose. And how did Bhishma awaken Jeevali?
DM: And you don't really know, I mean...
Kenzo: Do I—doubt—there's no—like, in our contract—I study this stuff, right?
DM: Um, not the—even the Lakan Mystai would not—this would not be part of their arcane knowledge.
Kenzo: Seeker, you're asking the right questions. So whatever those monks were trying to do 30 years ago...
Delwath: That—the other story the elves tell is that all of the human gods come from humanity's belief. Yes. Maybe the Awakened Soul is trying to awaken a god. Interesting.
Seeker: Mm-hmm. Shakun maybe is asleep in some sense, but that wasn't true 30 years ago.
Delwath: Maybe the Mystai felt they could influence the divine through their belief.
Seeker: Well, if something's gonna go spectacularly recently wrong, that sounds like such a thing.
Delwath: Or maybe it went spectacularly right. They were all lifted bodily to heaven.
Delwath: Whatever god they woke. When did—when did this guy come about? Grash, Grash.
DM: You don't really, I mean...
DM: You don't really know, except that the orc orc civil war is very recent.
DM: So if Grash provoked that, then presumably around the same time, right?

before: Delwath: It's a bad possibility.
Wellby: Speaking from experience, yes. But it's—it's a possible. I mean...

Kenzo: But I think—I think I'm at least given this... So at the end—just at the end of last session, I had the conversation with Tim where I was like, “Hey, I totally forgot to talk to the Pava and those dudes about the Order of the Awakened Soul. Can I retcon that?” And then we retconned it, and I was like, “Oh shit, this is a very critical piece of information. Fucking temple and this monastery of Bhishma is the Order of the Awakened Soul.” And then I was like, “Oh [garbled] what about like the potential like Rai guy but I saw on the first day?” So...
Delwath: We didn't—wait, what else did we care about the Order of the Awakened Soul?
Kenzo: Only for me, okay? Only for me and I'd only—only kind of—Kenzo only heard about it from [garbled] in the fucking dreamworld from like a robed dude with a jade hand, right?
after: Delwath: Anyway, perhaps we should go investigate.
Kenzo: Yes. Yes, we should.
Seeker: I support that idea, while we still have some afternoon light, you know.
Delwath: The heat of the day. Very good.
Wellby: For the first time in all of these wanderings, I start to worry that none of these events may be connected to each other.

interactions.title: Alesh’s warning recalled at the cliffs
lines: DM: As you approach the cliffs, you—you sort of have this eerie sense, like you're stepping into a place that is not quite right. And and now recall the stories of Alesh, that nobody goes to Kharsan because it's haunted. And you feel just a little bit of a cold tingle on the back of your neck as you cross within about five miles of the city, just on the edge of the cliff.

before: Delwath: And come up the river and then come approach from here, from the from the west.
DM: Okay, so.
Wellby: And I'm going to leave—I'm going to tell—before we go on—to tell Baxter that he's in charge of the horses and needs to watch out in case anyone comes.
Unknown: Okay.

DM: So, so you travel up the up the riverbed, and it's hot, drudgy work through this sort of soft sand, you know, occasionally being able to cling to the edge of the of the canyon wall, where, but you can get a bit of shade and relief, but with the sun directly overhead now there's almost no shade, and so it's it's just hot and tiring. Just hiking about this last five miles takes you takes you maybe an hour and a half, so it's about two o'clock when you arrive at the base of the cliffs and make your camp and, as you...
after: DM: Um, looking up the cliffs, I mean there's certainly scalable. It's not—it's not easy, there we go about 60 feet up, and there's not—you know, there's probably not a... Somebody would probably have to scale up and and find some somewhere to tie a rope, but it certainly could be done. They are sort of, you know, pretty—not so much steep as just soft, crumbly sandstone, and it might be tricky to find a solid handholds.
Unknown: We can switch.

DM: But you can see from the cliffs you know that that the temple in particular kind of looming on high. The—the—the temple building and the tower of the monks next to the Hall of Stories being the dominant landmarks that stand out, everything else being only one or a few, or two stories where those both stand between 40 and 70 feet high. You can see, you know, it take you about a half an hour to follow the curve of the river and and come up the slope. So what do you want to do?
Delwath: Like, we're gonna stick to the plan, right?
DM: Sure, follow the river.

interactions.title: The orc captain surrenders and answers questions
lines: Seeker: Alright, so I cast Suggestion.
Seeker: And the suggestion is to surrender, groveling, and tell us everything about the orc presence in this complex.
DM: Okay, that I would say that would seem reasonable to him. He failed the save badly. Orcs are not renowned for their wisdom.

DM: Nice. Um, so as you—as you come around the corner and the orc is beginning to flee from this enormous giant, Kenzo begins to shrink as the words reach the orc: “Drop your weapons and surrender.” And he turns and throws those weapons down and says, “I surrender,” in Common.
Seeker: Great. Somebody maybe tie him up? You guys yet.
Delwath: Yeah, let's take it back.
Seeker: Here, let's—let's bring him inside. Who knows...
Seeker: What else is going on around here?
Delwath: How many are in this compound?
Kenzo: What were you doing here?
Wellby: Are there other creatures here?
DM: “Just the ghosts.” He looks—he sort of blanches a little bit when he says that.
DM: I will not speak of those horrible things. They are—there, there are ghosts—their—spirits, and not—not friendly—not.
DM: They won't listen to Grash.
Delwath: Did they only come out at night?
DM: You like glances at the tower. He says, “They—they keep watch always.”
Delwath: Where do they keep watch?
DM: Tower. We can't go in.
Kenzo: What prevents you from going in?
DM: Ghosts. They will kill us.
Delwath: Why did—why did Grash send you here?
DM: See if anybody comes. Report back.
Wellby: Oh, when do you need to report back, or when are the guards changed here?
DM: Here days. We have supplies in that building. Tomorrow afternoon is our relief due.
Wellby: See—well the same number come to relieve you?
DM: Ghosts. I can't go in.
Wellby: The door. Which of the buildings have you been inside?

DM: “Just the bath and the dormitories. We feed the manticores, but...” And then he looks around. “We fed the manticores.” And you can tell the magic is still acting on him, and he is you know being cooperative because of the spell. “We fed the manticores, but they kept—they didn't like company.”
Delwath: Have you seen any gnolls?
DM: Not recently, not in the last few days. There were some that tried to poke their noses in Grash’s business. They were dealt with.
Kenzo: What else is here, other than...? Is there anything magic here? Is there any knowledge here, any items here it's guarding or protecting?
DM: He looks to Seeker kind of in desperation. “I—these are not questions I can answer.”
Seeker: Give him an encouraging look. “You're doing great.”
DM: He—he kind of looks a little bit concerned that that. “Grash... Grash has... There will be many. Grash will be powerful.”
Delwath: How goes the—what's the other guy—what's the other name? Uzgash, Uzgash. How goes the war against Uzgash?
Delwath: How many Uzgash have you fought?
DM: We fight them wherever we see them.
Delwath: Where do you see them most recently?
Delwath: Did any survive your your excursions?
DM: Of course not. We are—we are strong.
Wellby: What are you building on the plain to the north of here?
Wellby: Who's in the city? Have you seen Grash?
DM: Of course. We all worship him.
Wellby: What does he look like? Is he an orc?
DM: He is much stronger than an orc. He is—he is tall, giant, dark...
DM: Cloaked in shadowed and stronger than you can imagine.
Seeker: The—bigger than our friend was here when he was big a minute ago?
DM: He would crush your friend.
Delwath: Where did you live before Grash?
DM: East of here. Many of us lived there.

interactions.title: Bhishma’s story and the choice of sacrifice
lines: DM: You step into—step through the door, and everything fades to darkness. The hallway is dark, everything is dark, and even those of you with dark vision cannot see anything ahead, until a sort of faint light begins to glow from the walls, illuminating a scene painted on the wall sort of just to your right—so down the—turning right as you enter the corridor, down the corridor. It's faded in places, but still—still intricately detailed and and done by a master artist, and it shows a young woman, um...

DM: Kind of in a, you know, like that's a scene obviously painted to center on her, but giving also attention to the great mass of people that are following behind her, some on horses, some on foot, livestock with them, pulling carts loaded with just like the materials of home. This seems like a large group of of people taking their worldly possessions with them. And behind them sort of the painting kind of fades into this dark, roiling, shadowy mass.

DM: You feel, as you look at it, the wind in your hair, the hot desert air, the fear of what you've left behind, the cold ache of fleeing into the unknown and abandoning your home. And you sense a choice: to continue down this hallway, continue on the story of the woman you now realize is Bhishma, and be pulled along—to what end is unclear—or to turn back.
Kenzo: Well, if we're channeling our inner Wellby, there's not much of a choice here.
Seeker: To the senses of a just an especially vivid sort of magically enhanced mural?

DM: Almost—almost like a memory. A mural, yes, but also a memory, like—you can feel the wind in your hair. You can remember the feeling, that sort of ache of leaving your home and fleeing. It's not just visual stimuli.
Seeker: Is there a historical like evacuation?

DM: Ah, yes. The—the Dunmari were originally—originally lived far to the south and fled north in the—after the—many years ago, like after the fall of Drankor, the Drankorian Empire, but well before the Great War.
Seeker: Let's—let's go on. Think we need to know the story.
Delwath: Yeah, I mean, this feels like some sort of initiation into the mysteries of Bhishma that were accidentally following.

Wellby: I think—I think Wellby's gonna turn around. I think he's gonna say, like, “You know, I've been uncomfortable ever since we came through that door, because I feel like I just kind of surfed in behind you, Kenzo, and like I don't—like, I'm not a devotee of...”
Delwath: Yeah, Delwath is gonna go with Wellby.
Wellby: “I went into someone's house, and like I'm using the bathroom, and they're not even home. Like, this is just just you know...”
DM: Ma Seeker, what are you gonna do?
((Table conversation before continuing with Kenzo and Seeker))

DM: So as you continue down the hall, your companions turning back, you feel dragged along as if you are walking against your will. And the scene begins to change slightly. Now, rather than the dark mass behind you, you're passing through hostile terrain.

DM: The feeling of fear, the people coming to you for—for aid and comfort, pride in your brother being the hero, leading the charge against hob goblins cutting a path through the mountains to the safety on the other side. And coming to a wide, slow river, defensible—release—relief, the feel of wet earth beneath your feet after months traveling through dry, dusty land. The river valley, a place that could be home.

DM: But tinged with sadness, as the next scene show is the mass of people divided, some following you, some turning north, following the river to where it may lead, who knows. And while you can taste the—the dampness in the air and imagine the the sheep grazing and the horses spreading across these valleys, the split is painful still. You pass through another brief moment of darkness.
Seeker: Where are we geographically in that last scene?
DM: Ah, you are... So if you go here in Roll20, you are like right here.
Seeker: So that's the original—know—that's where the Dunmari settled before the plague.

DM: Well, we're getting to that. Um, turning now after the brief period of darkness, the next scene. And for a moment you sort of come back to yourselves, and everything is still black and you cannot see each other, but you can hear the sounds of your breathing again. And the sort of wind of the of the desert air, the rustling of grass, the sound of the water of the river lapping on the shores of its bank fades, until you are drawn forward again, unable to turn back.

DM: And you're riding west on horseback, spreading out, um, finding that the river itself is only a very narrow strip of fertile ground, and all around the land is ash. Um, riding further, coming to an empty river valley. The despair as the initial feeling of hope, um, turns to panic, the people questioning you, the taste of dust in your mouth, choking winds and ash blowing from the south. The sun disappearing for weeks at a time, the cold, the dark, the hunger pangs in your belly, the parched dryness in your throat.

DM: The children crying the fourth day after which the sun has not risen. The ash storms that that rise and blow across the land, bringing famine and disease, people dying. And you sense here you have another opportunity to turn back, which I presume neither of you take.

DM: And then standing at a place you feel in your heart is near where you are now. Then, as now, a dry river with no no water, clouds of dust, without even the perhaps harsh at times, but still sometimes beautiful colors of the desert sandstone. Um, just barren grey ash everywhere. Um, the doubt in your heart as people turn to you, and you have no answers for them.

DM: And then a miracle, the greatest miracle of your life. Jeevali’s tears, the rain comes. You are showered in praise, and yet all you can feel is shame and anger as the rains come and the ash is washed away and the land is cleansed and healed, and yet the goddess is dead, gone, nevermore to grace the land. As you rage and cry, the people rejoice and celebrate you and say you have saved them. And the land is healed and whole, and life goes on, except for the life of the goddess, who should be eternal and bring her blessings forever. And the scene fades again to darkness.

DM: And the lingering shame of that moment stays with you as you step forward again, again drawn against your will to a decision. Beginning construction of a monument, turning to pray, asking for anything, any way to trade your life for hers. Not caring that her brother Aagir has commanded your brother to slay in his name, not caring that the people are rejoicing as blood is shed and slaughter after slaughter after slaughter happens in Aagir’s name to take this land that your goddess has given her life for, so that only the Dunmari will benefit from her sacrifice and no one else.

DM: Turning to pray, turning away food, turning away water. The ache—the parched—your parched throat, the hunger, the pain, the agony as your life begins to fade away. As you encapsulate all of your belief in every moment of your life in the strength of this goddess, and ask whatever powers are out there to give it to her, to bring her back.
DM: And you sense you have one last moment to open your eyes and step back. And then a question posed to you: “Will you give your life for Jeevali?”
Seeker: So this is the initiation into the mystery of Bhishma, as a story told from perspective of Bhishma herself, right?
DM: That's the sense you get.
Seeker: And so there's a way in which it reflects the story of Bhishma self-sacrifice.
DM: All you know is you're standing in a dark corner—corridor being asked if you will sacrifice your life for Jeevali.
Seeker: Of what will happen if if we say yes or no?

Kenzo: Is it like weird, is it like unusual for Mystai like be be in multiple, you know...?

But you would never be in like a Lakan Mystai and a Jeevali Mystai, or something. But some of the gods are more closely connected. It's not—it's atypical, but it wouldn't be—like, Laka wouldn't be upset about it, like, your order wouldn't be mad.
Kenzo: But they're saying, “Would you give your life for Jeevali?” Yes, so, but this is part of the Bhishma initiation.

But what I'm saying is like does this feel like like you know, like is there, you know if if there's if if this is indeed like a like an initiation into a Mystai, and you know aka the Order of the Awakened Soul, I mean you know I kind of was feeling this one out like, if it's like feels right, I'll do it for sure. DM: He seems to be dead.

Seeker: Seeker immediately regrets not getting to do whatever Kenzo’s mind is doing right now, because I'm like, he's not really dead. He's like traveling somewhere, and I don't get to go. I'm—I start, like—like slapping your cheek a little bit. He's...
DM: He's, as far as you can tell that like.
DM: No breathing. His heart’s stopped. He's not breathing.
Seeker: I cast Healing Word. Oh, I'm out of—I cast first-level Healing Word.
DM: It doesn't do anything. He's—your healing energy is useless.

Seeker: Oh no. Kenzo, what did you do? I better run back and get the other guys, I guess. Or maybe... Oh, is there an initiation ritual that I know of where that would make you make it seem like you died?
DM: Make a Religion check. Um, I mean, you're not—you're not really an expert in secret societies.
DM: As your sort of standing here pondering this, you hear a deep gasp from Kenzo’s body.

DM: You are at one hit point. Use—you stand up, and around you, you see, um, the same room that Seeker sees as bare gray, bare stone, you see painted in bright colors. Um, a, like—a brightly colored arch way painted in flowers, leading into this pentagonal structure. So you're now right going back to the Monastery Bhishma, you're like right right here.

DM: And you're looking into a entry way to what looks like a—like a cloister. There's like a sort of walkway—a covered walkway around this central structure, which is open to the sky. And, well, to you, Seeker, looks like gray dark and grey and just kind of everything's flat and unpainted, to you, Kenzo, it's decorated with these brilliant paintings again of the life of Bhishma. There's a fountain flowing in the middle with clear water, and like everywhere you turn, you can see, ah...

Kenzo: Where's my notes? You see Kenzo just like kind of like stunned and like like becoming like very emotional and just looking like and what you see as like drab scenery and just saying, “So beautiful.”
Seeker: What—what happened, Kenzo? Were you locked away for 100 years in a shadow realm? Now...
Kenzo: I died. And Bhishma and Laka brought me back.
Seeker: Wow. Did you meet them?
Kenzo: Their—their presence was here, yes.

It begins to blow and begins to pick up sand, like a like a little mini kind of dust devil, sort of tornado-like, just small but kind of blowing around, collecting—collecting sand.

DM: And this continues for maybe five or 10 minutes as Kenzo remains kneeling in prayer, and the pitch of the wind almost seems to be singing a song as it—as it moves through this. And Kenzo, what—what you are seeing is not—is not wind picking up sand but um...

DM: Sort of emerging from the like like sparkles of like showers of water droplets kind of spraying up from the from the fountain and then turning into butterflies that are beginning to fly around sort of crystalline butterflies and circles around the around the courtyard. And they—they begin to—after—after a few moments, they sort of begin to do this dance and then drop. Their wings fall off, and they begin to fall to the ground. And Seeker, you see the sand began to fall in patterns on the ground.

DM: And it begins to spell out in Dunmari: “She is here with me. As always. But cannot reach Karawa. Something has been taken that should be there. Something that helps her reach the world. Find it and bring it back.”
Seeker: Can I see the writing?
DM: Yeah, yeah, you can see the writing.
Seeker: Holy shit, Kenzo, can you see that?
DM: To you, Kenzo, it looks like crystals that are sort of almost like multicolored ice crystals that formed out of the out of the wings of these butterflies, forming these words on the ground.
Kenzo: What is it? What connects with this world?
DM: You sense that the connection is fading, and this was—took a lot of energy already. But you—you get this sort of last lingering image in your mind of—of a beating heart.
DM: But not—not like a human heart. It's almost like—like a stone heart beating.
Kenzo: We need to find the heart of Shakun.
Seeker: Wow, well, that's good to know. I'm glad you asked. I am—I kneel briefly and bow my head to thank Bhishma.

DM: As the message is spelled out and then begins to fade, the um the crystals can then start to melt, and the fountain, although it doesn't disappear, begins to fade slightly, and the vibrancy of the colors begins to dim. And you have the sense that reaching into the world, even to just send a message directly like this, requires considerable energy on the part of the gods. And this is actually something you know from your Lakan studies.
DM: And maintaining the—the sort of power of the miracle that drives this illusion is—will be challenging for some time now for Bhishma.
Kenzo: Wow. So I'm a disciple of Bhishma now.
Kenzo: Wow. That was not—at—that—I was not expecting that to happen.

before: DM: Yeah, so—so there's always a public temple that anybody is welcome to go to, and is usually devoted to the, um, to, in this case, Bhishma or Shakun like—you've been into the sort of like chapel of Shakun at the the Shakun monastery in Karawa and similarly, the monastery Laka has like a big temple for Laka, which is also part library, but public, that anybody can go to it. Seeker: Talking about collecting...
after: Seeker: No, no.
Kenzo: Seeker, you were this close to joining.
Seeker: I—I feel like it all—it all went as it should have. I think it makes sense. Seeker's curiosity would drive him right to that kind of cusp, but then...
DM: I was like, wait, you're like, “Oh, I'm actually gonna die,” turns back.
Seeker: It's not actually cool, yeah. Well, step through an interdimensional portal, but not die, yeah.

interactions.title: Postgame clarification of the initiation
lines: DM: So many—you've had—you had a near-death experience, I would say right right.
Kenzo: But this time I actually died.
DM: You actually crossed over into the land of the dead and were brought back, yes.
Kenzo: Wow, wait. So when I—when I—when Kenzo like had his Lakan initiation he didn't—wasn't the same thing, that he also like died and come back?
Kenzo: Okay, so this is some like serious...

DM: Like some others, yeah. Now this is unique. Every initiation is completely different, although they the similarities, and I mean, technically you, you know normally initiates would be—would be—you would spend you know, a year studying and know what to expect.

DM: Right, and you would like you know pray and prepare yourself and you go into it, and you probably wouldn't suffer quite so much, right? But no—that—I never actually made up exactly what the Laka—but the Laka, I mean the Lakan Mystai are much more about sort of knowledge and study.

DM: He—well, yeah it would—it would be more like um, you know sort of you know, it's not just not just knowledge. It's also like sort of history, the passage of the year, keeper of traditions, like, you know I'd probably be more of—it wouldn't be an exam. That's too like sort of flat and—yeah—on—fine, but it would be like you know.

DM: Yeah, I think more be—so I think you would more—it wouldn't—it's not—the test would be—would be more guiding you towards like the hidden knowledge, right? So—so you'd probably have some—you probably would have had some experience of other planes at that point. Actually, probably the first time you ever experienced the Plane of Consciousness would have not been in your Rai dream. It would have been in your Lakan initiation.

DM: Because, like all of the secret knowledge you got from the Lakan Mystai is all about metaphysics and the sort of extraplanar world, and so I think it would probably be something like that, but you'd have to, you know um, you know, there would probably be some tests like, you'd have to understand...
